---
title: "Appendix: how the lab was built"
description: "The three-silo architecture, the systems and their pathologies, and the cost engineering that keeps a live cloud deployment at one cent."
---

The case study's findings, models, and memo all read from one unified
warehouse. This appendix is how that warehouse came to exist: the
architecture, the three systems the data was fractured into, and the
habits that keep the whole thing running for pennies. None of it is the
point of the project; all of it had to be true for the numbers to be
computable.

## Architecture

```text
             simulation engine (local Python, seeded, --scale dial)
                  │            │            │
          ┌───────▼──┐   ┌─────▼─────┐  ┌───▼──────────┐
          │ AWS S3   │   │ Neon      │  │ BigQuery     │
          │ auction  │   │ Postgres  │  │ marketing    │
          │ lake     │   │ CRM       │  │ exports      │
          └───────┬──┘   └─────┬─────┘  └───┬──────────┘
                  └──────┬─────┴─────┬──────┘
                         ▼           ▼
              DuckDB + dbt + Splink (unification, scored vs. ground truth)
                         │
                         ▼
         wide analytics marts · static dashboards · ML models
```

One seeded command regenerates everything at any scale: 1.5M consumer
records, 2.4M leads, 26.4M auction events, and 2.19M marketing messages in
about two and a half minutes at full scale. The simulator is calibrated
against three public datasets (iPinYou bid logs, LendingClub applications,
Criteo uplift), so its distributions are defensible, and the silo fracture
injects the identity pathologies that make unification genuinely hard.

## The three systems

The simulated marketplace's data is deliberately fractured the way real
marketplace data fractures:

| Silo | System | Grain | Identity scheme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Auction lake | S3, partitioned Parquet | one row per bid event | `lead_uuid` (UUIDv4) |
| CRM | Neon Postgres | one mutable row per lead | integer `lead_id` + hashed email |
| Marketing | BigQuery exports | one row per message | `contact_id` (MD5 of lowercased email) |

No silo contains another silo's key. The fracture adds heavy-tailed repeat
applications with channel-dependent identity drift (about 51% of
applications arrive under a drifted identity variant), about 5% orphaned
auction events from a simulated migration, timestamps logged in three
different timezones (UTC, naive US/Pacific, US/Eastern), and "conversion"
meaning three different things in three systems. Each pathology is
parameterized in the
[simulation engine](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/tree/main/simulation),
not hand-waved. How the systems are re-linked, and how well, is the
[identity modeling](silo-problem.qmd) page.

## The bill

At the close of silo deployment — three live cloud systems, roughly 3 GB
uploaded — the month-to-date bills read:

| Cloud | Month-to-date | Receipt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | **$0.01** | screenshot below |
| GCP | **$0.00** | screenshot below |

Both accounts run $10/month budgets with 50/80/100% alerts, configured before
any data moved — spend governance first, workload second.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![AWS billing console at phase close](../assets/img/aws-cost-2026-08-14.png){loading="lazy" fig-alt="AWS billing console screenshot showing one cent month-to-date"}

![GCP billing console at phase close](../assets/img/gcp-cost-2026-08-14.png){loading="lazy" fig-alt="GCP billing console screenshot showing zero dollars month-to-date"}
:::

The cheapness is engineered, not lucky. Four habits did the work.

## 1. Respect the write/read asymmetry

S3 PUT-class requests cost roughly 12x GET-class requests. Design
consequence: the auction lake is a few hundred *large* Parquet objects synced
once per deploy — never millions of small objects iterated remotely. A full
1.3 GB lake deployment costs under $0.02 in requests and about $0.03/month to
store.

## 2. Make the warehouse scan less

BigQuery prices queries by bytes scanned. A representative dashboard query
(one channel, one month, per-campaign open/click rollup) was benchmarked
before and after `PARTITION BY DATE(sent_at)` + `CLUSTER BY channel`:

| | Bytes scanned |
| --- | --- |
| Unpartitioned `messages` table | 124,325,982 |
| Partitioned + clustered | **11,430,092 (10.9x less)** |

At project scale both round to free. The point is the habit: extrapolated to
a 100x-scale table, the same query drops from ~12 GB scanned to ~1.1 GB —
the difference between exhausting the 1 TiB free tier in ~80 dashboard loads
versus ~900. Receipt:
[benchmark_receipt.json](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/silos/marketing_bq/benchmark_receipt.json).

## 3. Fit the free tier by measurement, not hope

The CRM silo's natural size (561 MB as generated) did not fit Neon's ~0.5 GB
free tier. Rather than pay the ~$15/month first paid tier, the deployed table
was re-engineered: two columns the entity-resolution ladder never uses were
dropped, and the email hash stored as 32-byte binary instead of 64-character
hex. Measured after the full 2.28M-row load: **0.470 GB logical — under the
tier with ~6% headroom**, hash round-trip verified exact. Thin headroom is a
managed risk: retention stays at the console minimum and any schema addition
re-measures first.

## 4. Push compute to the data

Egress ($0.09/GB beyond the free allowance) is the silent cost at real scale.
Local DuckDB reads the S3 lake directly over `httpfs` for development slices,
dashboards are built from small pre-aggregated extracts, and anything heavy
runs where the data lives. Development pulls stayed inside the free
allowance for the entire build.

## Steady state

With the working set at ~10 GB, the whole project idles at well under
$1/month — and the line-item model behind these numbers, including the
100x-scale extrapolation, is in
[the design document, Section 5](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/docs/design.md).
